content: Infants demonstrate a remarkable ability to make strong ontological inferences about the nature of the world and the types of entities it contains. Developmental psychology investigates the stages at which these metaphysical concepts are acquired. Infants infer that the world is composed of rigid objects that maintain continuity in both space and time. They perceive any cohesive, bounded surface that moves as a single unit to be a distinct object. When a solid object appears to pass through another, infants exhibit surprise, indicating a violation of their expectations about physical reality. By the age of less than one year, infants can distinguish between causal and non-causal events, even when these events share similar spatial and temporal properties. They differentiate between objects that move only when acted upon (inanimate objects) and those capable of self-generated motion (animate objects). Infants assume that the self-propelled movement of animate objects is driven by invisible internal states, such as goals and intentions, which they infer because these internal states are not directly observable. When an adult points to a novel object while uttering a word-like sound, toddlers typically assume that the word refers to the entire object rather than one of its parts. However, some of these inferences are not made by infants with autism, suggesting differences in cognitive development. Newborns, as far as current understanding allows, process raw sensory data without assigning it meaning. They lack the ability to differentiate between themselves and the external world. Self-awareness, widely believed by psychologists to emerge in mid-childhood, is thought to be present in only a few animal species. Tests for self-consciousness, such as the mirror test, involve placing a mark on a subject's body and observing whether they investigate the mark when viewing their reflection. If they do, it suggests an awareness of their own existence. In contrast, other species often interpret the reflection as another animal. Object permanence is a critical milestone in an infant's cognitive development. Numerous experiments have been conducted to study this concept, often involving a toy and a barrier that temporarily hides the toy (e.g., peek-a-boo). During the early sensorimotor stages, infants are unable to comprehend object permanence. Jean Piaget's experiments with infants led him to conclude that this awareness typically develops around eight to nine months of age. Before this age, infants do not understand that objects continue to exist when out of sight, which explains why they do not cry when their mothers leave their field of vision. This phenomenon is often summarized as out of sight, out of mind. A lack of object permanence can result in A-not-B errors, where children search for an object in a location where it should no longer be. Recent psychological studies also suggest that the understanding of three-dimensionality is not innate but must be learned during infancy through unconscious inference.
